rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the six-compound elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.

The maximum CRF is already achieved, with substantial resolution margin. Shorten the gradient at fixed temperature to seek a faster fully resolved separation and measure the critical pair’s sensitivity to gradient steepness.

Shorten the gradient another grid step while holding the solvent window and temperature fixed. The critical pair retained R = 2.46 at six minutes, suggesting a four-minute gradient may remain fully resolved and preserve the maximum CRF.

The four-minute gradient achieves maximum CRF, but the first pair is close to the resolution threshold. Raise temperature by 10 C to test whether faster elution can preserve full resolution and improve that pair’s selectivity.

Higher temperature worsened the critical pair, so test lower temperature to support a two-minute gradient. Reducing phi1 moderates gradient steepness; the last compound may elute during the final hold, which this run will assess.

Raise the final organic fraction one grid step to accelerate the last compound, which eluted during the hold. This tests whether the critical first pair retains full resolution despite the slightly steeper gradient.

Raise phi0 one step to reduce the gradient span while retaining the stronger final solvent that accelerated the last peak. This tests whether the shallower slope and shifted solvent window restore the first pair to R ≥ 1.5.

Shift both solvent endpoints upward one step, preserving the gradient slope that gave full resolution. The stronger final solvent should shorten the late peak’s hold-phase retention while testing whether the first pair remains sufficiently retained and resolved.

Shift the solvent window upward another grid step at unchanged slope and temperature. This should further accelerate the last peak while checking that the first pair preserves its current full-resolution margin.

Shift the solvent window upward one more step, retaining the slope and temperature that have maintained full resolution. Reaching the maximum final organic fraction should shorten the last peak’s retention while testing the first pair at a stronger starting solvent.

Raise only the starting organic fraction to shorten retention while making the gradient shallower. Check whether the first pair remains sufficiently retained and fully resolved as it approaches the gradient-delay region.
Increase temperature one grid step to shorten the last peak’s retention. The first pair now has R = 1.77, providing some margin against the loss of selectivity previously observed on heating.

Test the next stronger starting solvent at the temperature most favorable to the critical pair. This probes whether further window narrowing can shorten the separation without compressing the early peaks below R = 1.5; injection 12 remains the fastest fully resolved fallback.

Return phi0 to 0.30 to avoid the early-peak compression seen at 0.35. Test whether a shallower gradient ending at 0.90 offsets the critical pair’s temperature sensitivity, allowing full resolution at 35 C without excessive late-peak retention.

Lower the starting organic fraction to keep the first pair away from the near-unretained region, and use 30 C to recover selectivity. The narrower gradient span should help retain full resolution while providing a fast alternative to injection 12 with better early-peak retention.

Reduce phi1 one step from the fastest fully resolved method to test whether a shallower gradient adds resolution margin at only a small retention-time cost. Returning to 30 C should restore the critical-pair selectivity lost at 35 C.

Test one temperature step above the fastest fully resolved method to establish its speed–resolution boundary directly. The first pair is at risk based on injection 14; retain injection 12 as the maximum-CRF fallback if resolution drops below 1.5.

The faster-temperature boundary is now established, with injection 12 remaining the fastest fully resolved method. Test a narrower solvent window at 25 C for greater resolution margin while keeping the first peak comfortably retained and the separation short.

Raise phi1 one step from injection 18 to shorten the last peak’s hold-phase retention while retaining some of its resolution margin. This tests an intermediate speed–resolution compromise between injections 18 and 10.

Test the remaining cool-temperature neighbor of the fastest fully resolved method. The slightly shallower gradient may improve the critical pair’s resolution margin while keeping the last peak below three minutes and preserving maximum CRF.

Raise temperature one step from injection 18 to shorten late-peak retention while using its R = 1.85 margin to protect the critical pair. This tests a maximum-CRF alternative with better early retention than injection 12, which remains the fastest fully resolved method.

Narrow the solvent window one step from injection 20 to seek additional critical-pair resolution while keeping all peaks within roughly three minutes. The maximum CRF is already secured; injection 12 remains the fastest fully resolved method tested.

Raise temperature one step from injection 22 to shorten the last peak’s hold-phase retention, using its R = 1.90 margin to accommodate reduced selectivity. This should provide another fully resolved fast method, while injection 12 remains the fastest maximum-CRF result.

Test the lower-starting-solvent neighbor of injection 12 to determine whether better early retention can preserve full resolution at nearly the same speed. The first pair may fall slightly below threshold with the steeper gradient; injection 12 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-CRF method.

Use the final injection to test a better-retained early-peak alternative near injection 18, with sufficient expected resolution margin to preserve maximum CRF. Injection 12 remains the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method, with the last peak at 2.58 minutes.
